questions.prompt: A system uses a page size of 2 KB. Pages 0, 1, 2 and 3 are stored in page frames 1, 3, 2 and 0 respectively. Both physical and virtual addresses start from 0. What physical address corresponds to virtual address 2500?
questions.explanation: 2500 divided by 2048 gives page 1 with offset 452. Page 1 lives in frame 3, so the physical address is 3 x 2048 + 452 = 6144 + 452 = 6596.

questions.prompt: A system has 32-bit logical addresses, a 4 KB page size, and 4-byte page table entries. What is the size of a single-level page table for one process?

options.text: 16 MB
1 MB
4 MB
4 KB

questions.explanation: A 4 KB page needs 12 offset bits, leaving 20 bits of page number, so there are 2^20 entries. At 4 bytes each that is 4 MB per process — which is exactly why multi-level page tables exist.

questions.prompt: In a demand paging system, a memory access takes M units when the page is resident and D units when it causes a page fault. The measured average access time is X units. What is the page fault rate?

options.text: X / D
(X - M) / D

questions.explanation: With fault rate p, X = (1 - p)M + pD = M + p(D - M). Rearranging gives p = (X - M)/(D - M).

questions.prompt: The optimal page replacement algorithm evicts the page that:

options.text: Will not be used for the longest time in the future
Has been referenced the fewest times
Was loaded into memory earliest
Has not been used for the longest time in the past

questions.explanation: OPT looks forward, which makes it unimplementable in practice but useful as a lower bound on fault count. Looking backward at recency is LRU, and eviction by load order is FIFO.

questions.prompt: Which memory allocation problem does compaction address?

options.text: Thrashing
External fragmentation
Belady's anomaly
Internal fragmentation

questions.explanation: Compaction slides allocated regions together so scattered free holes merge into one usable block. Internal fragmentation is waste inside an allocated block and cannot be reclaimed by moving blocks around.

questions.prompt: What does the dirty (modified) bit in a page table entry indicate?

options.text: The page has been accessed recently
The page table entry is invalid
The page has been written to since it was loaded
The page is currently locked in memory

questions.explanation: A clean page can be discarded on eviction because an identical copy exists in the backing store; a dirty page must be written out first. This makes the bit a pure performance optimisation.

questions.prompt: Why is a multi-level page table preferred over a single-level one for a large address space?

options.text: It allows pages to be of variable size
It reduces the number of memory accesses per translation
It removes the need for a TLB
Page table pages for unused regions of the address space need not exist

questions.explanation: Address spaces are sparse, so most second-level tables are never allocated — the saving is in space. The cost is that translation now requires walking more levels, which is exactly why a TLB is essential.

questions.prompt: The locality of reference principle implies that the pages referenced by a process:

options.text: Tend to cluster in a small subset of its address space over a short interval
Are always accessed in strictly increasing address order
Are spread uniformly across its entire address space
Change completely on every memory reference

questions.explanation: Loops and contiguous data structures concentrate references into a working set. Without this property, caches, TLBs and demand paging would all fail to pay off.

questions.prompt: In a paging system with a TLB, the effective memory access time depends most directly on:

options.text: The number of processes in the ready queue
The TLB hit ratio
The size of the swap partition
The page replacement policy alone

questions.explanation: A TLB hit resolves the translation in cache time; a miss requires walking the page table in memory. Since the walk costs an extra access or more, effective time is dominated by the hit ratio.

questions.prompt: A process is allocated 3 frames and references pages 1, 2, 1, 3, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 1 with all frames initially empty. Using optimal page replacement, how many page faults occur?
questions.explanation: The seven faults are on 1, 2, 3, 7, 4, 5 and 6. Page 2 is the first victim because it is never referenced again; 1 and 3 are then kept, so the closing references to 3 and 1 are both hits.
